newsitem.title: UK: Lloyds Chemists says bids hit profits.
newsitem.headline: Lloyds Chemists says bids hit profits.

text.p: Lloyds Chemists on Wednesday said a 10-month bid battle between UniChem and Germany's Gehe AG for control of the British pharmacy group could reach a climax soon, but blamed uncertainty about its fate for lower annual profits.

Lloyds, also owner of healthfood retailer Holland & Barrett, saw pretax profits in the year to June 30 fall to 47 million pounds ($73 million) from 55.6 million. Sales rose to 1.13 billion pounds from 1.08 billion.
The dividend was held at 7.3 pence.

Chairman Allen Lloyd said the group's businesses had suffered from the uncertainty about the bids, launched early this year by UniChem and Gehe but allowed to lapse in March when they were both referred to Britain's competition watchdog the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.

"It is now more than eight months since since UniChem announced its first offer and during this time our businesses have been affected by the considerable uncertainty surrounding the bids," he said in a statement.
Lloyd was confident the rival bidders would meet conditions laid down by the MMC by an October 18 deadline, paving the way for fresh takeover offers.

The acquisition of Lloyds would give UniChem a dominant position in its home market while Germany's Gehe would be able to expand further in Britain after its purchase of drugs distributor AAH Plc last year.

The government said the takeovers could go ahead if the bidders, who each have about a third of the British wholesale drugs market, agreed to sell some of Lloyds' drugs wholesaling businesses. In August Lloyds said it had received numerous offers from prospective purchasers.
Managing director Michael Ward said, "We expect that the undertakings will be completed by October 18. We see no reason why we shouldn't achieve that."
He told Reuters in a telephone interview that the company had been under pressure from the bid uncertainty as had it stated in a profit warning in July.
After the warning analysts had suggested any new bids would be pegged below the original price of 500 pence a share.

But Ward said strong first quarter sales from its chemist and healthfood stores showed the underlying business was still strong. "I can't see any real reason for an impairment in the value of the business," he said.
Healthfood chain Holland & Barrett, which has benefited from the mad cow disease scare, saw profits rise 7.5 percent in the first half to a record 7.8 million pounds.
The main chemist division suffered a fall in profits to 43.1 million pounds from 45.1 million as margins slipped in the second half.
